passage: Pranav had been folding the paper boat since morning behind his father's tea stall at the bus stand. Twice it collapsed and twice he unfolded it, smoothing the creases with his thumb. He was making it for Vidya didi, who'd been ill and was going back to school tomorrow. He drew a small sun on the sail. When Vidya arrived, he held it out in both hands, avoiding her eyes. "It's lovely," she said. "I like the sun on the sail. And the sharp corners." Pranav's ears went red. "I did it three times," he said. Vidya smiled. "I can tell. I'll keep it on my desk."

qa.q: What did Pranav draw on the sail?
qa.a: He drew a small sun on the sail.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he handed over the boat, and what else might explain his red ears?
qa.a: He was probably proud and shy, since he avoided her eyes but told her he did it three times. The red ears might also be plain embarrassment at being watched.

qa.q: What kind of comment helps a child like Pranav most?
qa.a: A specific comment, like Vidya noticing the sun on the sail and the sharp corners, shows she looked closely and encourages him to keep making things.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel about receiving the boat?
qa.a: Vidya, who had been ill, probably feels cared for, since Pranav worked on it patiently for her and she says she will keep it on her desk.

grounding: A school-age child folds an origami boat with patience and care for a recipient, and a specific comment supports motivation.

passage: Beatriz had been building a cardboard model of the school bus for Lindiwe's birthday all week in the garage of their Lisbon house. She cut out windows, painted the wheels with yellow poster paint, and glued on paper passengers with names in tiny letters. When she brought it to the party, Lindiwe's uncle said, "Nice job!" and walked away. Beatriz's smile dimmed. Then Lindiwe crouched. "You put me at the front window! And the driver has my dad's moustache." Beatriz beamed. "I didn't know if you'd notice." Lindiwe set the bus on the shelf, next to her football trophy.

qa.q: What did Beatriz paint yellow on the model?
qa.a: She painted the wheels with yellow poster paint.

qa.q: What did Beatriz's dimmed smile suggest she felt after the uncle's comment, and why did she beam later?
qa.a: It suggests she felt a little disappointed that the comment was so general. She beamed when Lindiwe noticed the specific details she had worked hard on.

qa.q: What could Lindiwe's uncle say next time to encourage a child's effort?
qa.a: He could name something specific, like the painted wheels or the tiny names on the passengers, so the child knows the work was really seen.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel receiving the model?
qa.a: Lindiwe likely feels pleased and cared for because Beatriz put her at the front window and remembered her dad's moustache.

grounding: A child builds a model with pride, patience and care for the recipient, and specific comments support motivation better than general praise.

passage:
At the Saturday craft class in the community centre, Vasudha spent the whole hour on a pop-up card for her Nani's birthday. She cut a tiny paper house, folded it three times till the roof stood straight, and glued a small window that opened.
When the instructor, Joseph, came by, the other children waited for him to say "beautiful" like he always did. Instead he bent close. "You made the window open. And you folded the roof again and again till it stood up. That's patience."
Vasudha looked up quickly. "Nani always sits by her window."
Joseph nodded. "Then she'll see you thought about her."
Vasudha stayed late to add a little paper Nani inside the window.

qa.q: What did Vasudha add at the end?
qa.a: A little paper Nani inside the window.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha look up quickly when Joseph spoke?
qa.a: Vasudha felt surprised and pleased that Joseph noticed the opening window and her patient folding, which showed he really saw her effort.

qa.q: Why did Joseph's comment help more than saying "beautiful"?
qa.a: It named exactly what Vasudha did well, the opening window and the patient folding, which made her want to keep going and add more detail.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when she opens the card?
qa.a: Nani will likely feel loved and touched, seeing the house with a window and herself inside it.

grounding: At a craft class, a child makes a card with patience and care for the recipient, and specific praise motivates her.

passage:
My little brother Joseph built a bridge from ice-cream sticks for his school model contest. He glued each stick one by one, waiting for them to dry, for three whole evenings.
When Appa saw it, he said, "Very nice, very nice," and went back to his phone. Joseph's shoulders drooped a bit.
But when Appachan came in, he knelt down and looked from all sides. "These triangles make it strong. And you kept the sides even. How did you do that?"
Joseph started talking so fast I couldn't follow. He showed how he measured with a ruler and why he used triangles.
That night, he asked if he could make a bigger bridge for the next contest.
- Minakshi

qa.q: How many evenings did Joseph spend gluing the bridge?
qa.a: Three whole evenings.

qa.q: What does Joseph's drooping shoulders suggest?
qa.a: Joseph probably felt disappointed that Appa's quick "very nice" did not really notice his work.

qa.q: What made Appachan's comments more helpful than Appa's?
qa.a: Appachan noticed the triangles and even sides, which showed real interest and made Joseph excited to explain and try again.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see the difference in the two reactions?
qa.a: Minakshi saw that general praise left Joseph flat, but specific comments made him eager and proud.

grounding: An older sibling observes a child's model project and how specific praise motivates more than general flattery.

passage:
Monday: Amandeep tried to fold an origami crane for Yusuf, who was home with a broken leg. The paper tore on the fifth fold. He threw it in the bin.
Wednesday: After homework, Amandeep folded again with a video on the tablet, pausing after every step. His third crane looked like a bent chicken, but its wings could flap.
Saturday: He took his fifth crane, a blue one, to Yusuf's house. Yusuf turned it slowly. "You got the neck so thin! And the wing folds are sharp. How long did this take?"
Amandeep said, "Five tries." He was smiling so wide that Yusuf's mother laughed.

qa.q: What colour was the crane Amandeep took to Yusuf?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when he threw the torn paper in the bin?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and disappointed that his first try tore after so much effort.

qa.q: How did practising over several days help Amandeep?
qa.a: He learned by pausing after each step and trying again, which built both skill and patience.

qa.q: What was it like for Yusuf to receive the crane?
qa.a: Yusuf felt happy and impressed, noticing the thin neck and sharp folds, and appreciating the care it took.

grounding: Over several days, a child practises origami for a friend and receives specific, encouraging comments.

passage: Pranav, you want to know why I asked about your windmill's blades instead of just saying "nice"? When I was ten, I, Parveen, spent a whole week making a clay model of our mohalla for my Abba's birthday. Tiny doors, a mosque dome made from half an eggshell, even the tea stall's bench. At school the teacher glanced at it and said, "Very nice, very nice," and moved on. I felt as if I had shown a blank page. That evening Abba bent close and said, "You've put the crack in the tea stall bench, right where it is!" He noticed the crack! I glowed for days, and I made him three more models after that. So when you show me your windmill, beta, I look properly.

qa.q: What did young Parveen use for the mosque dome?
qa.a: Half an eggshell.

qa.q: How did young Parveen feel when the teacher said "Very nice, very nice"?
qa.a: Parveen felt disappointed and unseen, as if showing a blank page after a week of careful work.

qa.q: What turning point in the story kept young Parveen making models?
qa.a: Abba's specific comment about the cracked bench showed he had truly looked, and that made Parveen want to make three more.

qa.q: How might Abba have felt looking closely at the model?
qa.a: Abba was likely touched and proud that the whole mohalla had been captured so carefully, right down to the crack in the bench.

grounding: It shows a child's patient, proud craftwork for a parent, and how a specific comment motivates far more than general praise.
